meters.label: Pointers followed by the last find

frames.narration: Eight elements, 0 to 7, each its own group: every element's parent is itself, so every element is a root. find(x) follows parents to the root, and two elements are connected exactly when their roots are equal.
Edges arrive in the worst order: 0-1, 1-2, 2-3, and so on. A plain union hangs the first root under the second. After the 7 edges the parents form one chain: 0 points to 1, 1 to 2, and so on up to 7.

Now ask whether 0 and 7 are connected. find(0) follows 7 pointers to reach the root. Ask after every edge and the walks grow 1, 2, 3 and so on: 500,499 steps for 1,000 elements, about n squared over two.

Path compression: after find(0) has found the root, it points every node it passed straight at the root. The first find still costs 7 steps, but the chain has become a flat tree, and the next find(0) is a single step.

Union by rank attacks the cause. When joining, hang the shallower tree under the deeper one. A tree only gets taller when two equally tall trees meet, so a tree of height k holds at least 2 to the power k elements and the height never exceeds log2 of the element count. On random edges the deepest path drops from 87 to 5.

With both rules the cost per operation is close to constant: 4,777 operations for 1,000 random edges and 1,000 questions, against 109,799 for the plain version. The formal bound is amortized O(alpha(n)), the inverse Ackermann function, which is below 5 for any realistic n.

When the graph does not change, skip all of that. One traversal labels every component in n plus edges steps (5,000 here) and each question is a comparison. The catch is a graph that keeps growing: the traversal must start over after every edge, 1,499,499 steps on the chain workload, three times worse than plain union-find.

The limit: union-find only merges. It cannot remove an edge or split a group, because merging forgot which edge joined what and compression flattened the shape. If links also go away, you need a different structure, an offline method, or a recompute.
